item.title: France’s AI company Mistral opens Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore, plans 200 staff by 2027
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: Mistral, the French artificial intelligence (AI) company, has opened its Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore, operating as an extended science hub for developing sovereign AI models for governments and businesses in the region.
item.content:encoded:
Mistral, the French artificial intelligence (AI) company, has opened its Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore, operating as an extended science hub for developing sovereign AI models for governments and businesses in the region.

In a statement on Friday, Mistral reaffirmed its commitment to build sovereign AI capabilities, accelerate AI innovation amongst governments and enterprises, and drive long-term growth across the region. The office will operate as an extended Science Hub for the company, focused on developing sovereign AI models for three areas: public sector, high-tech manufacturing, and robotics.

As part of its long-term commitment to APAC, Mistral plans to more than double its workforce in Asia Pacific to 200 by 2027, building deep expertise across science, engineering, applied AI, and robotics. This strategic investment in talent will support the Hub’s ambition to accelerate the development, training and real-world deployment of sovereign AI models.

“The opening of Mistral’s Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore as an extended Science Hub reflects our long-term commitment to building sovereign AI capabilities in the region, for the region. Our ambition is to establish Singapore as a strategic location for empowering governments and enterprises across Asia Pacific to retain ownership of their infrastructure and intelligence, and translate these into lasting economic value and industrial competitiveness,” said Arthur Mensch, co-founder and CEO of Mistral.

Empowering Asia Pacific to Shape Its AI Future Through Sovereign AI

Mistral brings together frontier language models, physical AI, enterprise deployment, and sovereign compute infrastructure in an integrated AI stack. This enables enterprises and public institutions to harness frontier AI while retaining control over their data, intellectual property, and institutional knowledge.

Singapore, in particular, has played a pivotal role in shaping Mistral’s global innovation strategy by pioneering AI development. Collaborations with DSO National Laboratories and HTX were among Mistral’s first model-customization partnerships globally, generating valuable research insights and technological capabilities that contributed to shaping Mistral’s global product offering.

With the new Science Hub in Singapore, governments in APAC can benefit from an open-weight approach to develop, customize, and deploy AI within their own environments, aligned with local regulatory requirements and strategic priorities. This includes control across four dimensions: data sovereignty, ensuring sensitive information remains within designated boundaries; intelligence sovereignty, enabling customization and control; compute sovereignty, providing flexibility over infrastructure; and operational sovereignty, ensuring systems remain auditable and governable.

In high-tech manufacturing, Mistral aims to accelerate complex engineering simulations, optimize industrial processes and drive productivity and innovation. In robotics, Mistral is advancing intelligent models, including Robostral Navigate, an 8B model that enables robots to autonomously navigate complex environments using only a single RGB camera that is built entirely in-house, robot-agnostic and trained in simulation.

“Specialised AI models are a key part of the sovereign AI stack HTX has built to equip Home Team officers for rapidly evolving challenges. Working together with Mistral on our Phoenix models and Embodied AI initiatives has enabled us to ground innovations in operational contexts. As HTX scales our impact on public safety, these kinds of partnerships will become even more crucial. With Mistral opening its new APAC HQ in Singapore, we look forward to even more seamless collaboration to help the Home Team keep Singapore safe and secure,” said Ang Chee Wee, Chief AI Officer and Assistant Chief Executive (Digital & Enterprise), HTX (Home Team Science and Technology Agency), Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs.

“Mistral’s Asia-Pacific headquarters and expansion of its research and development activities in Singapore reinforces our position as a hub for frontier AI innovation. This investment will accelerate AI development and innovation across key industries and create opportunities for Singaporeans to work on cutting-edge AI technologies. We look forward to growing Singapore’s AI ecosystem and capabilities together with Mistral.” – Pee Beng Kong, Executive Vice President, Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB).

France’s Mistral raises €3B led by Samsung in largest European tech funding round

item.title: Sokin fully operational in Singapore after securing MAS licence
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Sokin, the global financial infrastructure firm, announced Wednesday its Singapore business is fully operational.
item.content:encoded:
Sokin, the global financial infrastructure firm, announced Wednesday its Singapore business is fully operational.

Since the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) licensed it as a Major Payment Institution under the Payment Services Act in April, Sokin said in a statement that it has been serving clients in Singapore while connecting its platform to local banking and payment infrastructure. Businesses can now use Sokin’s full range of regulated payment services from Singapore.

Following its licensing approval from MAS and commencement of full operations, the firm can offer businesses outside Singapore access to local Singapore dollar (SGD) accounts for receiving and making domestic payments without setting up a Singapore-incorporated entity.

Singapore-based businesses can also access locally domiciled accounts to receive SGD payments, with support for other currencies expected to be introduced in 2027.

It is noted that much of the demand for local payments in Asia-Pacific now comes through embedded finance, as fintechs, marketplaces and software platforms build payments and accounts into their own products.

By building on Sokin, those platforms can offer their customers cross-border transfers, Singapore dollar accounts and payment acceptance, instead of securing their own license and banking relationships market by market.

“A Major Payment Institution license is the highest bar Singapore sets, and clearing it means our customers in Asia are working with a counterparty that MAS holds to that standard.

“Licenses take years to earn, and no amount of money shortens that. Singapore is where much of the money between Asia and the rest of the world moves, and now we serve that flow under our own license,” said Vroon Modgill, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Sokin.

Singapore is Sokin’s regulated base for the Asia-Pacific region, and the company plans to double headcount in its Singapore office by the end of the first quarter of 2027. Its MAS license joins those the company holds across 36 countries.

Sokin said holding licenses in its own name, rather than operating under third-party regulatory arrangements, gives the firm a direct relationship with the regulators that license it.

It noted that licensed infrastructure is also critical to stablecoins and agentic treasury. It enables stablecoins to settle in local currency and agents to act on AI-prepared payment instructions.

This year, Sokin launched stablecoin accounts and settlement and introduced a range of agentic treasury capabilities, including an MCP connector that lets finance teams send payments through the AI tools they already use.

The MAS license extends that infrastructure to Singapore, giving businesses across the Asia-Pacific region the licensed base these services depend on, said the firm.

item.title: AIS and Huawei jointly launch the first Autonomous Networks Innovation center outside China
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: China's telecommunication firm Huawei and Thailand's telecom operator AIS have jointly launched the AIS Agentic Transformation Joint Innovation Center, the first Autonomous Networks (AN) innovation center outside China.
item.content:encoded:
China’s telecommunication firm Huawei and Thailand’s telecom operator AIS have jointly launched the AIS Agentic Transformation Joint Innovation Center, the first Autonomous Networks (AN) innovation center outside China.

This marks a new phase in their strategic collaboration in the AN sector. Their successful practices across multiple high-value scenarios provide a robust support for AN Level 4 implementation and the commercial deployment of AI-driven AN capabilities around the world, Huawei said in a statement on Tuesday.

It is noted that Huawei and AIS started their strategic collaboration on AN in 2022. AIS regards AN as the core strategy of its intelligent infrastructure transformation and has defined a clear evolution roadmap for AN.

The innovation center focuses on high-value scenarios across maintenance, optimization, and operations, demonstrating the achievements of both parties over the past four years from six dimensions: strategic collaboration, operations and maintenance (O&M) efficiency improvement, user experience enhancement, network resilience enhancement, sustainable development, and capability openness.

The center covers full-scenario practices of single-domain and cross-domain agents across wireless, datacom, optical, and core network domains.

In terms of efficiency improvement, the cloud core agent achieves a 90 percent automated diagnosis rate, and IP single-domain autonomy boosts field O&M efficiency by 15 percent.

In terms of user experience, the automated complaint diagnosis rate reaches 70 percent, with customer complaints reduced by 10 percent year on year.

In terms of network resilience, CORESpirit enables hierarchical fault autonomy and minute-level service recovery. In terms of sustainable development, network energy consumption is reduced by over 3%.

Additionally, the launch of the first IP and core network single-domain autonomy solution and collaboration solution for cross-domain agents and RANSpirit outside China marks a significant AN Level 4 transformation from single-scenario autonomy in phase 1 toward multi-scenario collaboration in phase 2.

The innovation center provides industry partners with a platform for exchange and live-network demonstrations, facilitating the large-scale commercial deployment of AN Level 4 network capabilities.

With this innovation center, Huawei and AIS will continue to enhance AN Level 4 network capabilities across high-value scenarios, develop more innovative end-to-end network-level autonomy solutions, and enhance open collaboration through the OpenAN open-source project, thereby comprehensively accelerating the large-scale deployment of AN Level 4.

TM Forum’s Autonomous Network Levels (ANL) provide a standardized maturity model for telecom operators to assess and plan their automation and autonomy journey. Levels range from fully manual operations at Level 0 to full autonomy at Level 5. Level 4 describes a highly autonomous network with intent-driven operations, predictive analytics, and AI-based closed-loop management.

Huawei Malaysia partners CelcomDigi to accelerate talent development in future technologies

item.title: DNB and Ericsson validate AI-driven 5G fault management
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Malaysia's DNB and Ericsson secured TM Forum Level 4 validation for AI-driven management of major 5G radio network fault categories.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s state-backed 5G network operator Digital Nasional Berhad and Ericsson have secured TM Forum Level 4 autonomy validation for three categories of artificial intelligence-driven radio access network fault management.

The validation covers equipment, communications and environmental faults across DNB’s nationwide radio access network. The companies said those three categories account for 98 percent of incidents encountered in day-to-day operations.

The assessment covered three of the five fault categories in TM Forum’s radio access network fault-management evaluation. Level 4 denotes highly autonomous operations within the validated scenarios; it does not mean every part of the network runs without people. DNB said human governance and operational control remain part of the system.

DNB and Ericsson said the production system uses intent-based, policy-driven closed-loop operations to detect, diagnose and resolve network issues. Agentic AI and decision intelligence translate operational objectives into remediation actions with minimal human intervention, while retaining governance and operational controls.

The companies said the approach combines AI-powered root-cause analysis with autonomous decision-making and human oversight. It is designed to shorten fault-resolution times, improve operational efficiency and strengthen network resilience.

The latest assessment extends DNB and Ericsson’s earlier work on autonomous network operations. In October 2025, the partners received what they described as the world’s first TM Forum Level 4 autonomy validation for 5G service assurance, covering throughput management. Ericsson said at the time that the capability had been active in DNB’s network for two years and used intent-based operations, generative AI and digital twins.

DNB said the new fault-management validation places it among six operators publicly listed by TM Forum with two Level 4 or partial Level 4 autonomous network validations as of October 2026. The comparison is limited to operators that agreed to publish their validation results.

The development comes as DNB expands the capacity and capabilities of Malaysia’s wholesale 5G network. In July, the operator said it was activating additional spectrum and infrastructure upgrades while investing in 5G-Advanced and AI-driven autonomous network management.

Ken Tan, DNB’s chief technology officer, said the operator’s first AI use case focused on network performance and that it is now applying those lessons to fault management. David Hagerbro, head of Ericsson Malaysia, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, said intent-based operations are intended to improve network quality, resilience and management efficiency.

DNB carries most of Malaysia’s 5G mobile traffic through a wholesale network used by the country’s mobile operators. The companies said more intelligent fault handling should support service reliability and provide a stronger foundation for enterprise 5G applications.

DNB ramps up 5G capacity as it enters next phase

item.title: Singapore’s DBS partners Circle expand institutional access to USDC in Asia
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: DBS, Singapore’s largest bank by assets, and Circle Internet Group, Inc., an internet financial platform company and the issuer of USDC, announced Wednesday a partnership to strengthen stable coin infrastructure across Asia and expand institutional access to USDC.
item.content:encoded:
DBS, Singapore’s largest bank by assets, and Circle Internet Group, Inc., an internet financial platform company and the issuer of USDC, announced Wednesday a partnership to strengthen stable coin infrastructure across Asia and expand institutional access to USDC.

DBS said in a statement that this partnership brings together Circle’s regulated stable coin infrastructure and global reach with DBS’ digital asset capabilities, financial strength.

These combined capabilities aim to support growing demand from institutions for a trusted and secure bridge between traditional and blockchain-based financial systems, enabling them to move and manage value across both environments with greater confidence.

Under the partnership, eligible institutional clients can directly mint and redeem USDC through DBS, enabling them to diversify their reliance on secondary market liquidity to meet their USDC needs.

This provides institutions with greater flexibility and certainty when using the stablecoin to support treasury, settlement and liquidity management requirements.

The arrangement also enables 24/7 USD-USDC settlement when minting and redeeming the stablecoin through DBS. This means institutions can manage liquidity across fiat and digital asset environments seamlessly, without the constraint of banking hours and cut-off timings.

The collaboration comes as corporations and financial institutions increasingly explore tokenized money to modernize financial operations and improve the movement of value across markets.

According to DBS’ report, The Great Rewiring: Money in a new order, 88 percent of large corporations are already deploying or piloting tokenized money use cases, while more than three-in-five are already adopting, or planning to adopt, stablecoins.

“Institutions are increasingly looking to tokenized money to manage liquidity more efficiently and support their growth across new markets. This partnership meets that demand by bringing together Circle’s regulated stablecoin infrastructure and global reach with DBS’ trusted banking, liquidity and digital asset capabilities in Asia,

“We believe the future of financial services will be multi-modal and multi-instrumental, with different forms of tokenized money serving different needs. By supporting USDC, alongside other trusted tokenized money instruments, we are providing institutions greater choice in how they move and manage value, based on what best serves their needs,” said Evy Theunis, Head of Digital Assets, Institutional Banking Group, DBS.

Kash Razzaghi, Chief Commercial Officer, Circle, said financial institutions are increasingly looking for trusted ways to access stablecoins and integrate blockchain-based infrastructure into their financial operations.

“By combining Circle’s regulated stablecoin infrastructure with DBS’ institutional banking and liquidity capabilities, our partnership represents an important step in expanding institutional access to USDC across Asia, while strengthening the banking infrastructure supporting its global adoption,” he added.

The partnership also builds on DBS’ and Circle’s participation in Project BLOOM, an industry initiative led by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to enable the safe, seamless and scalable use of tokenized money.

Through their participation in the initiative, both organizations are contributing to industry efforts to support interoperability between different forms of tokenized money and financial networks, reinforcing Singapore’s position as an important center for digital asset innovation.

Singapore central bank issues tokenized bills using wholesale CBDC on test network

item.title: Sokin starts full payment operations in Singapore
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Sokin has made its full regulated payments platform operational in Singapore after obtaining a Major Payment Institution license from MAS.
item.content:encoded:
Cross-border payments company Sokin has made its full regulated payment-services platform operational in Singapore after receiving a Major Payment Institution license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore earlier this year.

The company said in a Nov. 18 announcement sent directly to TNGlobal that businesses in and outside Singapore can now use its regulated cross-border transfer, local Singapore dollar account and payment-acceptance services. Sokin has been serving clients while connecting its platform to local banking and payment infrastructure since receiving the license in April.

Sokin’s regulatory disclosure identifies Sokin Capital Singapore Pte. Ltd. as the licensed local entity. The MAS Financial Institutions Directory lists the company as a Major Payment Institution authorized for account issuance, domestic and cross-border money transfers, merchant acquisition and e-money issuance.

The Singapore launch gives overseas businesses the option to use a local Singapore dollar account to receive and send domestic payments without establishing a Singapore-incorporated entity, according to Sokin. Singapore companies receive locally domiciled accounts for Singapore dollar payments, with support for additional currencies planned in 2027.

Sokin is positioning the local operation as an infrastructure layer for fintechs, marketplaces and software companies that embed payments and accounts in their own products. The company said those customers can use its regulated services instead of building separate licensing and banking arrangements in each market.

Singapore will serve as Sokin’s regulated base for Asia-Pacific. The company plans to double the headcount at its Singapore office by the end of the first quarter of 2027, although it did not provide the current staff number or an investment figure for the expansion.

Sokin said it holds licenses across 36 countries and processes more than $11 billion annually. It also offers stablecoin settlement and agentic treasury tools, including a connector that can initiate payments through artificial intelligence tools. Those operating and volume figures were supplied by the company and were not independently audited in the announcement.

The rollout follows other recent international payment companies using Singapore’s licensing framework as a regional base. Earlier in November, TNGlobal reported that Pyvio secured its own Singapore Major Payment Institution license for five regulated payment services.

Sokin did not disclose Singapore customer numbers, expected transaction volumes or pricing tied specifically to the expanded local operation.

Pyvio secures Singapore major payment institution licence

item.title: JOYY third-quarter revenue rises 15.6 percent to $624.6 million
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: JOYY reported third-quarter revenue of $624.6 million as BIGO Ads and SHOPLINE grew, while operating cash inflow reached $102.2 million.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore-based technology company JOYY reported third-quarter 2026 net revenue of $624.6 million, up 15.6 percent from a year earlier as advertising and commerce operations expanded.

Revenue also increased 5.7 percent from the previous quarter, according to the company’s unaudited results for the three months ended September 30.

Social Entertainment revenue rose 8.8 percent year on year to $441 million. BIGO Ads revenue increased 39.6 percent to $145.7 million, while ecommerce platform SHOPLINE recorded revenue of $37.8 million, up 24.7 percent. The three businesses accounted for most of the group’s reported revenue during the period.

Net income from continuing operations attributable to JOYY’s controlling interest was $59.6 million, compared with $62 million in the same period a year earlier. Non-GAAP operating income increased 14.6 percent to $46.6 million. JOYY uses non-GAAP measures that exclude items including share-based compensation, impairment charges and certain acquisition-related expenses.

The company generated $102.2 million in operating cash flow during the quarter. Cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash, short-term deposits and investments totaled $2.94 billion at the end of September. The balance provides funding for product investment and shareholder returns, although the company did not issue a new capital-allocation target with the quarter’s results.

JOYY said it had returned $536 million to shareholders from the start of 2026 through November 13, comprising $319.8 million of share repurchases and $216.2 million of dividends. The returns form part of a plan announced earlier this year to distribute about $1.5 billion through dividends and buybacks through 2028.

The results extend the company’s revenue growth from the second quarter, when it reported $590.8 million in total revenue. Advertising and SHOPLINE again grew faster than the larger social entertainment segment, while net income remained below the prior-year quarter.

JOYY said it will continue investing in artificial intelligence features, advertising technology and SHOPLINE’s merchant services while managing spending across its social entertainment operations. The company has not provided audited full-year results for 2026.

JOYY Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results: Total Revenues Increase to US$590.8 Million, Driven by Growth Across Core Businesses

item.title: XTransfer, VPBank and SmartPay plan Vietnam payment links
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: XTransfer, VPBank and SmartPay will develop payment, collection and FX services for SMEs trading between Vietnam, China and ASEAN markets.
item.content:encoded:
XTransfer, Vietnam Prosperity Joint Stock Commercial Bank and Vietnamese fintech SmartPay have agreed to develop domestic and cross-border payment services for small and medium-sized businesses trading between Vietnam, China and other Southeast Asian markets.

The three companies signed a memorandum of understanding at the Singapore FinTech Festival, according to an announcement from VPBank. Their initial work will focus on trade-related payments and collections along Vietnam-China and Vietnam-ASEAN corridors.

The partners plan to connect systems through application programming interfaces and digital platforms, with the aim of automating transaction processing and moving it closer to real time. They will also develop foreign-exchange conversion services for businesses using the payment links.

One model under consideration would let Vietnamese buyers pay in Vietnamese dong through domestic payment infrastructure. Overseas suppliers would receive funds through XTransfer’s cross-border network after currency conversion and settlement. The companies said the model is intended to reduce payment friction and improve cash-flow management, but they did not announce pricing, participating banks, supported currencies beyond the proposed dong collection flow or a commercial launch date.

The proposed service addresses a specific regional trade use case: Vietnamese SMEs often buy from suppliers in China and ASEAN while operating primarily in local currency. VPBank would contribute its local banking and SME capabilities, SmartPay its Vietnamese payment infrastructure, and XTransfer its cross-border collection and settlement network.

XTransfer said it serves more than one million business customers and processed more than $60 billion in total payment volume in 2025, citing research firm CIC. Those figures were supplied by the company and were not presented as independent measures of the wider cross-border payments market.

The MOU is an agreement to develop and test the services rather than a completed deployment. VPBank’s announcement said the parties expect the collaboration to support more efficient digital payments for importers and exporters and help Vietnamese businesses participate in regional supply chains.

B2B cross-border trade payment platform XTransfer opens Malaysia office as strategic Southeast Asia hub

item.title: Oxygen7 and Mesh prepare digital asset QR payments in Bhutan
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Oxygen7 and Mesh plan an invitation-only Bhutan beta that connects digital asset wallets to local QR payments with merchant settlement in ngultrum.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore-listed OxPay Financial’s Oxygen7 unit and payments network Mesh are preparing a Bhutan launch that would let international travelers fund local QR-code purchases from supported digital asset wallets while merchants receive Bhutanese ngultrum.

Under the partnership, Mesh will provide wallet connectivity and payment orchestration for NomiOne, Oxygen7’s new consumer travel wallet. Oxygen7 will operate the application and arrange local payment and settlement, according to a company announcement reviewed by TNGlobal.

The companies said Bhutan will be the first market. The initial service will support participating merchants using DK Bank’s QR payment infrastructure. Travelers will be able to connect an existing supported wallet, scan a merchant QR code and authorize a payment, while the merchant is settled in local currency without directly holding or managing digital assets.

The division of responsibilities is intended to keep the consumer interface and local settlement arrangements with Oxygen7 while Mesh links NomiOne to external wallets and funding sources. The partners described the service as non-custodial, meaning the product is not designed to take custody of a traveler’s digital assets before a transaction.

Oxygen7 is targeting an invitation-only beta by the end of November 2026. Broader availability on mobile app stores will depend on testing and operational readiness, the company said. It did not disclose expected transaction volumes, fees, the number of merchants in the beta or the list of supported digital assets.

The rollout builds on Oxygen7’s regulated presence in Gelephu Mindfulness City. The Gelephu Financial Services Office directory lists Oxygen7 as an active provider of money services, with its license dated April 29, 2026. OxPay previously said the license allows the subsidiary to provide merchant payment and business remittance services in the financial hub.

The financial hub has been developing rules for digital-asset services and cross-border payments as part of Bhutan’s effort to attract regulated financial technology activity. Oxygen7’s license applies to its activity in that jurisdiction and does not by itself authorize the product in other markets.

OxPay said NomiOne is designed for travelers who want to use digital assets through familiar local payment rails while preserving local-currency settlement for merchants. After the initial Bhutan rollout, Oxygen7 intends to evaluate other markets where local payment infrastructure and regulatory arrangements support a similar model.

Thunes Expands Real-Time Payouts to Bhutan, Unlocking the Nation’s Remittance Market

item.title: Skyro expands reusable credit line to partner checkouts in the Philippines
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Skyro will let eligible Philippine users apply their reusable SkyroCredit limit inside participating merchant checkouts and partner apps.
item.content:encoded:
Philippine consumer finance company Skyro is expanding its reusable SkyroCredit line to partner checkouts and merchant applications, extending the product beyond Skyro’s own mobile app.

The company said the rollout will begin in the Philippines and allow approved customers to use available credit directly within a participating merchant’s checkout flow. Merchants can integrate the service through a webview or an application programming interface.

SkyroCredit gives eligible users a reusable limit that replenishes as they repay outstanding balances. Customers can choose how much of the available limit to use for a purchase, while participating merchants receive payment through Skyro’s embedded financing infrastructure.

The checkout version uses the same approved credit line rather than requiring a separate application for every transaction, according to Skyro. Purchase terms, repayment schedules and available limits remain subject to the customer’s account and the merchant’s implementation.

Skyro said it works with more than 3,000 partners across over 11,000 stores and has issued more than 500,000 loans through embedded partnerships. The company also said it has about 7 million registered customers and a loan portfolio exceeding $200 million. Those figures were supplied by Skyro and were not independently audited in the announcement.

The checkout rollout is intended to reduce the steps between credit approval and a purchase. Instead of drawing funds into a separate account or leaving a merchant application, an eligible user can select SkyroCredit during checkout, subject to the product’s terms and available limit.

For merchants, the integration places financing inside an existing digital sales journey. Skyro said the webview option is intended to reduce implementation work, while the application programming interface offers partners more control over how the financing option appears in their checkout.

The expansion follows Skyro’s recent product launches in its home market, including a cashback program introduced in October. Skyro has not disclosed a complete list of participating merchants for the new checkout service or a timetable for coverage across all partners.

The company said the merchant integration will be deployed in stages, with the Philippines serving as the initial market. Availability will depend on individual partner implementation and customer eligibility.

Philippines’ Skyro launches pioneering cashback program in home market
